Olpiny Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Ołpiny, Poland

Not demolished. Jews are recorded in Ołpiny from 1785, peaking at 477 residents in 1870 before declining to 185 (7%) by 1921; most were deported to the Gorlice ghetto in 1942 and murdered in Gorlice, Stróżówka, or Bełżec. This cemetery, likely established in the 19th century alongside the local Jewish community's development, uniquely contains within its grounds a separate WWI War Cemetery No. 35, holding four Russian Imperial soldiers and two Austro-Hungarian soldiers. In a notable 1917 legal case, two local shepherds were tried in Jasło for knocking over tombstones and defacing others with feces and charcoal crosses. Local residents further contributed to the cemetery's WWII-era destruction, using tombstones for construction. Since 2015, the AntySchematy 2 Foundation has managed the site, relocating recovered tombstones and running educational programs with local students.
